**Phenomenology** — the first-person description of experience as a method — the philosophical tradition (Husserl, Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty), its use in the sciences of mind, and the theories that take their data from it (group: philosophy; ADR-016).

| [LIT-209](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-209.md) v2 | The Phenomenology of Ritual Resistance: Colin Kaepernick as Confucian Sage | Walsh (2021), DOI-10.1007/s11712-020-09759-4. | [LIT-445](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-445.md) | From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | Oizumi, Albantakis & Tononi (2014), PLoS Computational Biology 10(5):e1003588. IIT 3.0 states five axioms of experience (existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion), turns each into a postulate about mechanisms in a state, and identifies an experience with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a "complex". Exclusion makes a complex a local maximum of integrated conceptual information Φ over all overlapping sets of elements, so complexes cannot overlap and no subset or superset of a complex is conscious. Worked logic-gate examples show minor complexes beside a major one, an inactive network that is conscious, a minimally conscious photodiode, and a feed-forward "zombie" functionally equivalent to a conscious system. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md)), equations excepted; worth reading as the formal statement of the exclusion postulate that Schwitzgebel's 2014 manuscript ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) attacks: "of all overlapping sets of elements, only one set can be conscious", a complex being a local maximum of Φ against every overlapping set. It is IIT's anti-nesting principle, stated as a postulate and motivated only by the phenomenological exclusion axiom; the paper's Occam's-razor argument is given for exclusion within a mechanism, not between systems. It also says plainly that function does not fix consciousness, which is IIT's answer to whether agency built from parts brings experience with it. |
| [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. The minimal self splits into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which come apart in involuntary movement and, after Frith, in schizophrenic thought insertion when a forward comparator fails. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". Read in the author's preprint. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md)), in the author's preprint, not the typeset article; worth reading as the paper that set the minimal self against the narrative self for cognitive science, and for the split of the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which it ties to Frith's comparator model of schizophrenic thought insertion. It is a short review: the empirical support is cited, not shown, and its own proposal, the self as "the sum total of its narratives", is offered in two paragraphs. |
| [LIT-463](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-463.md) | Subjectivity and Selfhood: Investigating the First-Person Perspective | Zahavi (2005), MIT Press. Per its publisher, a defence of the self against neuroscientists and philosophers who doubt it, arguing that "the notion of self is crucial for a proper understanding of consciousness" and that experience, self-awareness and selfhood cannot be understood apart. It uses Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty to give an account of the "experiential givenness of the self" for philosophy of mind, cognitive science, developmental psychology and psychiatry. Its chapters run from self-awareness and phenomenal consciousness through time-consciousness and reflection to self and other, theory of mind, autism and embodiment. | [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Worth reading as the most complete short statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT): more of the machinery than "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)), in particular the six constraints, the degrees of transparency, and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". It states the theory and its predictions; the evidence is cited, not shown, and the neural sections say how little is known. |
| [LIT-571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-571.md) | Participatory sense-making: An enactive approach to social cognition | De Jaegher & Di Paolo (2007), Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 6(4):485–507. Coordination between coupled systems is cheap and common. When patterns of coordination and the course of an encounter shape each other, the interaction acquires its own operationally closed, precarious organization. Social interaction is then regulated coupling between autonomous agents that constitutes an autonomous relational organization without destroying the agents' autonomy. Because sense-making is embodied in movement, interactors can coordinate their sense-making, along a spectrum from modulated individual sense-making to jointly created meaning. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-456](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-456.md)), from the published version posted on De Jaegher's own site. Worth reading as the founding statement of participatory sense-making. A social interaction is defined as regulated coupling between autonomous agents that itself becomes an autonomous organization in the relational domain, without destroying the agents' autonomy; coordinating sense-making in interaction can generate meanings neither individual had. The argument is conceptual, illustrated by everyday cases and by the perceptual-crossing experiments; nothing is measured in the paper. |
